processing: Made into oolong the Anxi way, with partial oxidation and tight rolling into pellets.
harvest_season: As with other Anxi oolongs, mainly spring and autumn.
appearance_dry: Larger pellets than Tie Guan Yin, made from noticeably coarser, bigger leaf.
appearance_liquor: Usually a pale yellow-gold, as is typical of light Anxi oolong.
appearance_wet: Big, fairly thick leaves unfold, clearly coarser than Tie Guan Yin.
taste_profile: A strong aroma over a forceful cup, bolder in style than Tie Guan Yin. Florals are typical of the Anxi class, though detailed notes for this cultivar are scarce.

brewing.notes: The usual Anxi routine. Because this is a strong tea, keep the early steeps short, or use a little less leaf.

vintage_note: Usually sold as the current year's spring or autumn tea, as is normal for Anxi oolongs in the light style. It is often grouped under the sezhong label. Drink light lots within about a year.
description:
Mei Zhan is one of Anxi's native cultivars and belongs to the sezhong group, the local name for oolongs made from anything other than Tie Guan Yin.

The leaf is big, which you can see at once: the pellets are larger and coarser than Tie Guan Yin.

In the cup it is loud rather than subtle, with a strong aroma and a forceful body. Treat it with short steeps, because it pushes harder than Tie Guan Yin does.

It rarely has the fame or price of Tie Guan Yin, and that makes it a good value way to learn the Anxi cultivars side by side. Ask for the season and year when buying, and try it next to Huang Dan to see how far apart two sezhong can be.
history: Mei Zhan is regarded as native to Anxi, but its naming and early history are poorly documented. In the 1950s China's commodity inspection authorities divided Anxi oolong into Tie Guan Yin, sezhong and oolong grades for grading purposes, and Mei Zhan went into the sezhong group, where it is still placed.
